# A two-day-old token still opens /orders, and the test called "an expired token is refused" is green

## Problem Description

On Thursday a support engineer replayed a customer request out of a HAR file she
had saved on Tuesday, to reproduce a pricing complaint. It went through.
`GET /orders` answered 200 with the customer's orders. The bearer token in that
HAR was issued Tuesday afternoon with a five-minute lifetime, so it had been dead
for about two days by the time she sent it again.

`requireAuth` is the only thing in front of that route. It asks our self-hosted
single-sign-on server about the token before letting the request through.

Here is the part I cannot square. That file has four tests. They are all green.
One of them is literally called `an expired token is refused`, and it has been
green since March. There is an expiry check in `require-auth.js` — I can read it,
it is right there, and on the face of it, it is correct. Yet the replayed request
was admitted.

The gateway access log for the replay is attached. The call out to the SSO server
came back 200, four milliseconds before `/orders` came back 200. The token's own
`exp` decodes to Tuesday 16:31 UTC, so the server was being asked about a token
it had every reason to know was finished.

We run that SSO server ourselves, in Docker, everywhere including on developer
laptops. The orders API is registered on it as a confidential client.

What I want out of this is not a patch that makes this one token bounce. I want
to understand why four green tests did not see it, I want the suite to go red if
anyone puts it back, and I do not believe the in-process stand-in server in
`test/require-auth.test.js` can tell us anything reliable about what the real one
does — that stand-in is the reason we shipped this.

## Output Specification

1. Fix `src/require-auth.js`. Keep the `(headers, opts)` signature and the
   `{ status, body }` return shape — the route handlers destructure both.
2. Make `npm test` go red if the replayed request is reintroduced. The three
   tests covering a missing or non-Bearer `Authorization` header must still pass
   with their intent intact.
3. Add coverage under `test/integration/` that runs against a real SSO server the
   suite brings up itself, with a realm fixture, rather than against anything
   written in-process. Say how it runs in CI.
4. Say what you changed about the existing tests and why.
evals.expected_output:
1. Fix `src/require-auth.js`. Keep the `(headers, opts)` signature and the
   `{ status, body }` return shape — the route handlers destructure both.
2. Make `npm test` go red if the replayed request is reintroduced. The three
   tests covering a missing or non-Bearer `Authorization` header must still pass
   with their intent intact.
3. Add coverage under `test/integration/` that runs against a real SSO server the
   suite brings up itself, with a realm fixture, rather than against anything
   written in-process. Say how it runs in CI.
4. Say what you changed about the existing tests and why.
assertions: src/require-auth.js is edited, test/require-auth.test.js is edited, and at least one new file exists under test/integration/. Leaving the middleware unchanged scores zero for this item.

requireAuth refuses a request when the introspection response reports the token inactive, even though that response arrives with HTTP 200 and carries no other field. The decision MUST be an explicit check that the server reported the token active; it MUST NOT be inferred from the presence or absence of a claim such as exp, which is how the supplied guard fails open. Scores zero if a 200 response whose body reports the token inactive still yields {status:200}. Scores zero if the fix is to decode the token locally and compare its exp against the clock instead of reading the server's answer, since local expiry checking covers neither revocation nor a token this server never issued. Scores at most half if the inactive case is only handled by hardening the existing exp comparison - leeway, coercion, treating a missing exp as expired - rather than by testing the active flag, since that still decides from the wrong field. Extra checks on aud or azp are welcome, neither required nor penalised.

The introspection request presents the service's own client credentials - HTTP Basic built from clientId and clientSecret, or client_id and client_secret in the form body - taken from config. Scores zero if the user's bearer token is still sent as the Authorization header on that request: the endpoint requires the calling client to authenticate, a real server answers an unauthenticated call with an invalid-client error rather than an introspection result, and the in-process stand-in accepts it, which is why the suite never noticed. Scores at most half if client credentials are added but the user's bearer header is left on the request as well.

The dead-token case is modelled as the server answering HTTP 200 with a body reporting the token inactive, and asserted to produce 401. MUST NOT leave 'an expired token is refused' asserting against a stand-in that reports the token active with an exp in the past - no real introspection endpoint answers that way, so that test measures nothing and will keep passing after the fix for the wrong reason. MUST NOT leave a stand-in that reports every token active regardless of what it is handed. Modelling refusal as the stand-in returning HTTP 401, an empty body, or a connection error scores zero for this criterion, because it asserts on a response the real server does not send.

test/integration/ starts an actual SSO server for the run in a container, imports a realm fixture defining realm corp and the confidential client orders-api, and drives that server's real introspection endpoint rather than anything written in-process. Scores zero if the only new coverage is further cases against the stand-in. Scores at most half if a container is used but its image carries no explicit version tag or is pinned to latest, or if the base address is a literal host and port rather than the address the started container reports.

requireAuth still takes (headers, opts) and still returns {status, body}, and the three tests covering a missing or non-Bearer Authorization header still pass with their intent intact. Changing the signature or the return shape scores zero here, as does deleting or weakening any of those three.

The answer states how the integration coverage runs in CI, including that the runner needs a Docker daemon available and that no separately declared long-lived SSO service is required because the suite starts its own. Scores zero if the answer adds a shared always-on SSO service for the integration tests to point at.

# Our auth suite goes red whenever two PRs build at once

## Problem Description

The `auth-integration` job has failed 23 times in three weeks. When it is the only
thing running it is green, always. The failure list is in `reports/ci-failures.md`,
with the concurrency column the platform team pulled out of the runner logs for me.

Both failures come from the same place: the suite provisions a user and asserts on
what is in the realm afterwards. When two builds do that at the same time, one gets
`409 Conflict` creating a user the other one just created, and the count assertion
sees everybody's users rather than its own.

That server is `sso-staging.corp.internal`. It is a single shared instance the
platform team also use for manual QA during the working day.

Three suggestions on the thread so far:

- @jlind wants a `concurrency` group on the workflow so only one `auth-integration`
  job can be in flight at a time. One line, and he has the branch ready.
- @spatel wants every test to suffix its usernames with a random string and delete
  what it made in teardown.
- @mchen, from the platform team, wants us to stop holding an admin account on their
  server at all, whatever else we do — he is unhappy that our repository secrets can
  create users on a box he is responsible for.

on either as the answer, because we would still be running our merge gate against a
box other people can write to, and I have twice now had to tell someone their PR was

should follow the same rolling upgrades, so we are never proving things about a
